summary: The blueprint for the classical Habiro-ring roadmap: the cyclotomic completions R[q]^S = lim R[q]/(f), f in the monoid generated by Φ_n, n in S (HC.1), factorial expansions and finite-precision arithmetic (HC.2), evaluation and Taylor maps at roots of unity (HC.3), adjacency of orders and Habiro's rigidity theorems with their exact hypotheses (HC.4), modules, components and inverted primes (HC.5), and the exported interface with explicit acceptance examples (HC.6). Corrected by REV-HabiroCyclotomicCompletions. The source is Kazuo Habiro, 'Cyclotomic Completions of Polynomial Rings', Publ. RIMS 40 (2004), read in the published version whose hash is recorded, with the arXiv preprint for the normalised expansion and its uniqueness, which the published version dropped; eighteen mistakes are listed, sixteen in Habiro's paper (two in stated results: Corollary 5.1's 'in particular' and a missing connectedness hypothesis in Theorem 6.2; and a proof step of Theorem 6.2 that fails over ℤ[i]) and two in Wagner's q-Witt vectors. The reviewed audit AUDIT-17 records every layer as not built; the pinned libraries supply cyclotomic polynomials, division by monic polynomials, Hasse derivatives and the polynomial Taylor shift, power-series substitution under nilpotence (so the p-adic re-expansion uses PowerSeries.eval₂Hom under topological nilpotence), adic completion and PolynomialModule, but nothing named Habiro. In HC.5 the completion of a polynomial module is exact for every coefficient ring, so no derived-limit correction occurs there; the derived completion of modules with torsion belongs to HabiroRings HR.2 and is compared in one node. The Chinese remainder decomposition is stated under comaximality, which is stronger than non-adjacency and agrees with it for Noetherian domains; over Q every pair of orders splits (Habiro §7.5), and over Z[1/Δ] the completion is a product of infinitely many domains, on which evaluation at all roots of unity is still injective while each Taylor map is not. The comparison with the Habiro ring of the rational field is performed by HabiroNumberFields HB.6. In HC.1–HC.4: q is a unit of every R[q]^S (not only when 1 ∈ S); the factorial products (q; q)_N have leading coefficient (−1)^N, so the normalised digits come from successive division by q^{n+1} − 1; the map R[q] → R[q]^S is injective exactly when S ≠ ∅ or R = 0; adjacency is reflexive (c_{n,n} = 0); Habiro's §3 and Lemmas 3.1 and 4.2 are nodes, so the proof of Theorem 4.1 closes. Nothing here is formalised; implementationStatus is unchecked throughout.

nodes.title: The cyclotomic index monoid
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R and a set S of positive integers, the cyclotomic index monoid Φ*_S(R) is the submonoid of the multiplicative monoid of R[q] generated by the cyclotomic polynomials Φ_n(q) ∈ R[q], n ∈ S (Mathlib's cyclotomic n R, the image of the integral cyclotomic polynomial). It is a set of polynomials, not of exponent vectors: over F_2, Φ_2 = q + 1 = q − 1 = Φ_1, so Φ*_{1}(F_2) = Φ*_{2}(F_2). Its elements are monic, hence non-zero-divisors of R[q]; it is directed by divisibility (f and g divide fg); it is monotone in S; a ring map h : R → R' maps Φ*_S(R) into Φ*_S(R'); for finite S the powers (∏_{n∈S} Φ_n)^j are cofinal in it; and it has a cofinal divisibility chain g_0 ∣ g_1 ∣ ⋯, for instance g_N = ∏_{n∈S, n≤N} Φ_n^N. Its least element is the empty product 1, and Φ*_∅(R) = {1}.
hypotheses: R is commutative and unital; S ⊆ ℕ_{>0} is arbitrary, possibly empty or infinite. In Lean S : Set ℕ, and 0 ∈ S is harmless because Mathlib's cyclotomic 0 R is 1.
Divisibility is a preorder on Φ*_S(R); nothing here needs antisymmetry.
proofSteps: Define Φ*_S(R) as Submonoid.closure of {Φ_n : n ∈ S}.
Monicity: induction on the closure, with Polynomial.cyclotomic.monic and Monic.mul.
Directedness: f ∣ fg and g ∣ fg.
Functoriality: Polynomial.map h is multiplicative and map_cyclotomic sends Φ_n over R to Φ_n over R'.
Finite S: ∏Φ_n^{e_n} divides (∏_{n∈S} Φ_n)^{max e_n} (source, p. 1131).
Cofinal chain: g_N ∣ g_{N+1}, and ∏Φ_n^{e_n} divides g_N as soon as N is at least every n and every e_n that occur.
acceptance: Every element of Φ*_S(R) is monic.
A ring map carries Φ*_S(R) into Φ*_S(R').

nodes.title: The S-cyclotomic completion
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R and S ⊆ ℕ_{>0}, the S-cyclotomic completion R[q]^S is the ring of compatible families (x_f)_{f∈Φ*_S(R)}, x_f ∈ R[q]/(f), such that x_g maps to x_f under the canonical surjection R[q]/(g) → R[q]/(f) whenever f ∣ g; that is, R[q]^S = lim_{f∈Φ*_S} R[q]/(f) (Habiro (1.1) and (3.1)). It is an R[q]-algebra and an R-algebra. It comes with surjective projections π_f : R[q]^S → R[q]/(f), with the map ι : R[q] → R[q]^S, p ↦ (p mod f)_f, satisfying π_f ∘ ι = the quotient map, and with extensionality: x = y as soon as π_f(x) = π_f(y) for every f. Degenerate cases: R[q]^∅ = 0, because the only index is 1 and R[q]/(1) = 0, and in general the least index 1 contributes the zero ring as initial stage. The map ι is injective if and only if S ≠ ∅ or R = 0; no other injectivity is asserted here, and the injectivity of the restriction maps between completions is HC.4. For n ∈ S and R ≠ 0, Φ_n is not a unit of R[q]^S, because π_{Φ_n} sends it to 0 in the non-zero ring R[q]/(Φ_n); in particular R[q]^S is not a field, and no formal division by Φ_n exists.
hypotheses: R is commutative and unital; S ⊆ ℕ_{>0} is arbitrary, possibly empty or infinite.
The index set is Φ*_S(R) of HC.1/the-cyclotomic-index-monoid, a set of monic polynomials directed by divisibility.
The only hypothesis for injectivity of ι is S ≠ ∅ (or R = 0); it is unrelated to the adjacency conditions of HC.4.
proofSteps: Define R[q]^S as the R[q]-subalgebra of ∏_{f∈Φ*_S} R[q]/(f) cut out by the equations x_f = (image of x_g) for f ∣ g, using Ideal.Quotient.factor and Ideal.span_singleton_le_span_singleton.
The projections are the coordinate maps; ι is the algebra map; π_f ∘ ι is the quotient map, so π_f is surjective.
Extensionality is equality of families.
Injectivity of ι for n ∈ S: if ι(p) = 0 then Φ_n^k ∣ p for every k; for R ≠ 0 a non-zero p cannot be divisible by a monic polynomial of larger degree (Monic.not_dvd_of_degree_lt), so p = 0.
Non-units: π_{Φ_n}(Φ_n) = 0, and R[q]/(Φ_n) ≠ 0 because Φ_n is monic of positive degree and R ≠ 0.
acceptance: Two elements with the same image in every R[q]/(f) are equal.

nodes.title: The finite quotients of the completion
nodes.statement: For every f ∈ Φ*_S(R) the projection π_f : R[q]^S → R[q]/(f) is surjective with kernel f·R[q]^S. Hence R[q]^S/(f) ≅ R[q]/(f); multiplication by f is injective on R[q]^S, so f is a non-zero-divisor of R[q]^S; an element of R[q]^S is divisible by f in R[q]^S exactly when its f-component vanishes, and then the quotient is unique; and for every x ∈ R[q]^S there are b ∈ R[q] and c ∈ R[q]^S with x = ι(b) + f·c.
hypotheses: R commutative; f ∈ Φ*_S(R), hence monic and a non-zero-divisor of R[q].
proofSteps: Surjectivity: π_f ∘ ι is the quotient map.
If π_f(x) = 0, then for each g ∈ Φ*_S the class x_{fg} ∈ R[q]/(fg) maps to 0 in R[q]/(f), so x_{fg} = f·y_g for a class y_g ∈ R[q]/(g), unique because f is a non-zero-divisor.
The y_g are compatible along divisibility (cancel f again), so y = (y_g) ∈ R[q]^S, and (f·y)_h = x_h for every h.
Conversely f·R[q]^S ⊆ ker π_f since π_f(f) = 0; the decomposition x = ι(b) + f·c takes b a lift of π_f(x).
Multiplication by f is injective: if f·x = 0 then f·x_{fg} ∈ (fg), so x_{fg} ∈ (g) because f is a non-zero-divisor of R[q], and x_g = 0 for every g.
acceptance: ker π_f = f·R[q]^S for every f ∈ Φ*_S.
R[q]^S/(Φ_n) ≅ R[q]/(Φ_n) for n ∈ S.
In ℤ[q]^ℕ an element vanishing at every primitive n-th root of unity is divisible by Φ_n, and ℤ[q]^ℕ/(Φ_n) ≅ ℤ[q]/(Φ_n) ≅ ℤ[ζ_n].
Multiplication by Φ_n is injective on R[q]^S for n ∈ S.

nodes.title: The topology of the completion, its completeness and its universal property
nodes.statement: Give R[q]^S the inverse-limit topology, induced from the product of the discrete rings R[q]/(f), f ∈ Φ*_S. Its open ideals f·R[q]^S = ker π_f form a basis of neighbourhoods of 0, so the topology is linear and R[q]^S is a topological ring; R[q]^S is complete and separated for it (Tau Ceti's IsCompleteSeparated), ι has dense image, and R[q]^S ≅ lim_f R[q]^S/(f). Universal property: give R[q] the linear topology whose basic open ideals are (f), f ∈ Φ*_S. For every topological commutative ring T that is complete and separated for the group uniformity of its topology, and every ring map φ : R[q] → T continuous for that topology (for every neighbourhood U of 0 there is f ∈ Φ*_S with φ((f)) ⊆ U), there is exactly one continuous ring map ψ : R[q]^S → T with ψ ∘ ι = φ. Equivalently R[q]^S is the separated completion of R[q] for the Φ*_S-topology, and the universal property is that of Mathlib's UniformSpace.Completion.
hypotheses: T complete and separated for the group uniformity of its topology.
φ continuous for the Φ*_S-linear topology on R[q], not for an adic topology.
proofSteps: The compatibility equations are closed conditions in the product of discrete rings, so R[q]^S is a closed subring; products of complete separated rings are complete separated, and so are closed subrings (Tau Ceti IsCompleteSeparated.pi and IsCompleteSeparated.of_isClosedEmbedding).
The basic open sets ker π_f are the ideals f·R[q]^S (HC.1/the-quotients-of-the-completion), so the topology is linear and the ring operations are continuous.
Density: x + ker π_f meets ι(R[q]) because π_f ∘ ι is surjective.

Existence of ψ: for x choose p_f ∈ R[q] with ι(p_f) − x ∈ ker π_f; the net φ(p_f) is Cauchy because p_g − p_f ∈ (f) for f ∣ g; its limit is ψ(x). Equivalently, identify R[q]^S with UniformSpace.Completion of R[q] and use UniformSpace.Completion.extensionHom.
Uniqueness: continuous maps into a separated ring that agree on a dense subring agree (Tau Ceti UniformSpace.Completion.ringHom_ext_of_continuous).
acceptance: IsCompleteSeparated holds for R[q]^S for every R and S.
ι has dense image, and the ker π_f are open and closed.
Continuous maps into complete separated rings extend uniquely along ι.

nodes.title: The completion computed along a mutually cofinal family of ideals
nodes.statement: Let (g_i)_{i∈I} be a family of polynomials of R[q], directed by divisibility, such that every (g_i) contains some (f) with f ∈ Φ*_S and every (f), f ∈ Φ*_S, contains some (g_i). Then the map R[q]^S → lim_i R[q]/(g_i) induced by the identity of R[q] is an isomorphism of topological rings compatible with the maps from R[q]. Consequences: for finite S, R[q]^S ≅ AdicCompletion (span{∏_{n∈S} Φ_n}) R[q], so R[q]^{1} ≅ R[[q − 1]]; R[q]^S ≅ lim_{S'⊆S finite} R[q]^{S'} (the source's (3.2)); and, for S = ℕ_{>0}, the factorial system and the system of the (q^m − 1)^k (HC.1/cofinality-of-the-factorial-products).
hypotheses: Mutual cofinality of the two systems of principal ideals is the whole hypothesis; the g_i need not lie in Φ*_S (for instance P_N for odd N).
proofSteps: Mutual cofinality gives compatible maps between the two systems of finite quotients, and hence maps of limits in both directions; they are inverse because both composites are compatible with the maps from R[q] and the limits are separated with dense image of R[q].
The topologies agree because the two families of ideals are mutually cofinal (Tau Ceti SubmodulesBasis.topology_eq on R[q], transported to the completions).
Finite S: the powers of ∏_{n∈S} Φ_n are cofinal (HC.1/the-cyclotomic-index-monoid), and AdicCompletion is the limit over those powers.
(3.2): the Φ*_{S'} for finite S' ⊆ S exhaust Φ*_S.
acceptance: R[q]^{1} ≅ R[[q − 1]] and, for finite S, R[q]^S ≅ AdicCompletion (span{∏_{n∈S} Φ_n}) R[q].
R[q]^S ≅ lim_{S' finite} R[q]^{S'}.

nodes.title: The factorial polynomials (q; q)_N
nodes.statement: For N ≥ 0 the factorial polynomial is P_N(q) = (q; q)_N = ∏_{i=1}^{N}(1 − q^i) ∈ R[q], with P_0 = 1 and P_{N+1} = P_N·(1 − q^{N+1}). Its constant term is 1 and its leading coefficient is (−1)^N. So P_N is not monic for odd N, while (−1)^N P_N = ∏_{i=1}^{N}(q^i − 1) is monic, of degree N(N+1)/2 when R ≠ 0. Grouping q^i − 1 = ∏_{d∣i} Φ_d gives (−1)^N P_N = ∏_{d=1}^{N} Φ_d^{⌊N/d⌋}, so (−1)^N P_N ∈ Φ*_{ℕ>0}(R) and P_N generates the same ideal. nodes.title: Cofinality of the factorial products, and which completion this is not
nodes.statement: Let S = ℕ_{>0}. Every f = ∏_d Φ_d^{e_d} ∈ Φ*(R) divides P_N as soon as N ≥ max_d d·e_d, because Φ_d occurs in (−1)^N P_N with multiplicity ⌊N/d⌋; and every (−1)^N P_N lies in Φ*. So the ideals (P_N) are cofinal in the system (f), f ∈ Φ*, and the map R[q]^{ℕ>0} → lim_N R[q]/(P_N) induced by the identity of R[q] is an isomorphism of topological rings (Habiro, introduction). Likewise the ideals ((q^m − 1)^k), m ≥ 1, k ≥ 0, are cofinal, since (q^m − 1)^k = ∏_{d∣m} Φ_d^k ∈ Φ* and ∏Φ_d^{e_d} divides (q^L − 1)^E with L the lcm of the d and E = max e_d. Hence R[q]^{ℕ>0} ≅ lim_m R[q]^∧_{(q^m − 1)}, the limit of the (q^m − 1)-adic completions over m ordered by divisibility (Habiro p. 1136 with (3.2)). Over ℤ the multiplicity count is sharp: Φ_d^e ∣ P_N if and only if d·e ≤ N.
hypotheses: S = ℕ_{>0}. For a general S the P_N do not lie in Φ*_S; the analogue is any cofinal chain of Φ*_S (HC.1/the-cyclotomic-index-monoid).
Over every R only the implication N ≥ max d·e_d ⇒ f ∣ P_N is used; the sharp form is over ℤ (over F_p distinct products of cyclotomic polynomials can coincide).
Sign: P_N ∉ Φ* for odd N; (−1)^N P_N ∈ Φ* generates the same ideal.
proofSteps: Multiplicities: (−1)^N P_N = ∏_{d≤N} Φ_d^{⌊N/d⌋} (HC.1/the-factorial-polynomials).
Cofinality of (P_N): ⌊N/d⌋ ≥ e_d when N ≥ d·e_d.
Cofinality of ((q^m − 1)^k): (q^m − 1)^k ∈ Φ*, ∏Φ_d^{e_d} ∣ (q^L − 1)^E, and (q^m − 1)^k ∣ P_{mk} since Φ_d occurs in P_{mk} with multiplicity ⌊mk/d⌋ ≥ k for d ∣ m.
Apply HC.1/completion-along-a-cofinal-family to both systems; for the second, group the indices (m, k) by m to obtain the limit of the (q^m − 1)-adic completions.
Sharpness over ℤ: the Φ_d are pairwise non-associate irreducibles of ℤ[q], so the multiplicity of Φ_d in P_N is exactly ⌊N/d⌋.
acceptance: f ∣ P_N for N ≥ max_d d·e_d; over ℤ, Φ_d^e ∣ P_N if and only if d·e ≤ N (checked for 300 random f: the least N equals max d·e_d).
R[q]^{ℕ>0} ≅ lim_N R[q]/(P_N), compatibly with ι.

nodes.title: The full completion is neither q-adic nor (q − 1)-adic
nodes.statement: Let R ≠ 0. There is no ring isomorphism R[q]^{ℕ>0} ≅ R[[q]] and no ring isomorphism R[q]^{ℕ>0} ≅ R[[q − 1]] compatible with the maps from R[q]. Indeed Φ_1 = q − 1 is a unit of the q-adic completion (constant term −1) but not of R[q]^{ℕ>0}, and Φ_6 = q^2 − q + 1 is a unit of the (q − 1)-adic completion (Φ_6(1) = 1, as for every order that is not a prime power) but not of R[q]^{ℕ>0}. More strongly (Habiro, Proposition 6.1), for a subring R of Q̄ and an infinite S there is no ideal I of R[q] for which the identity of R[q] induces an isomorphism R[q]^S ≅ lim_j R[q]/I^j. For finite S, by contrast, R[q]^S is the (∏_{n∈S} Φ_n)-adic completion; in particular R[q]^{1} = R[[q − 1]].
hypotheses: R ≠ 0 for the unit arguments; for R = 0 all these rings are zero.
Proposition 6.1 needs R ⊆ Q̄ and S infinite, as in the source.
The statements concern isomorphisms compatible with the maps from R[q] (the source's 'induced by id_{R[q]}').
proofSteps: A ring map compatible with R[q] sends Φ_n to Φ_n and units to units; Φ_n is not a unit of R[q]^{ℕ>0} (HC.1/the-cyclotomic-completion).
Φ_1 has constant term −1, a unit, so it is a unit of R[[q]]; Φ_6(1) = 1 (Polynomial.eval_one_cyclotomic_not_prime_pow), so Φ_6 = 1 + (q − 1)h is a unit of R[[q − 1]] (Φ_6(1 + t) = 1 + t + t^2).

Proposition 6.1 (source proof, p. 1140): for a non-zero f ∈ I choose m ∈ S with Φ_m ∤ f; then Φ_m ∤ f^j for all j, so no power of I lies in (Φ_m). The case I = 0 is excluded because ι is not surjective for infinite S (source issue E3).
The finite case is HC.1/completion-along-a-cofinal-family.
acceptance: Φ_1 is a unit of R[[q]] and not of R[q]^{ℕ>0}; Φ_6 is a unit of R[[q − 1]] and not of R[q]^{ℕ>0}.
Proposition 6.1 is stated with R ⊆ Q̄ and S infinite.
R[q]^{1} = R[[q − 1]] is recorded, so the non-example is not over-generalised to finite S.

nodes.title: Functoriality in the coefficient ring and restriction in the order set
nodes.statement: Coefficient change: a ring map h : R → R' sends Φ_n over R to Φ_n over R' (map_cyclotomic), hence Φ*_S(R) into Φ*_S(R'), and induces a continuous ring map h^S : R[q]^S → R'[q]^S with π_{h(f)} ∘ h^S = (R[q]/(f) → R'[q]/(h(f))) ∘ π_f and h^S ∘ ι = ι ∘ h_q, and with id^S = id and (h' ∘ h)^S = h'^S ∘ h^S. Restriction: for S' ⊆ S, Φ*_{S'} ⊆ Φ*_S and the identity of R[q] induces a continuous ρ_{S,S'} : R[q]^S → R[q]^{S'} with ρ_{S,S} = id, ρ_{S',S''} ∘ ρ_{S,S'} = ρ_{S,S''} and ρ_{S,S'} ∘ ι = ι, so S ↦ R[q]^S is a presheaf of rings on the discrete set ℕ_{>0} with R[q]^∅ = 0. The two functorialities commute: h^{S'} ∘ ρ_{S,S'} = ρ_{S,S'} ∘ h^S. Injectivity and surjectivity of h^S are HC.1/coefficient-change-injective-and-surjective; injectivity of ρ is HC.4. Base change: on each finite quotient R[q]/(f) ⊗_R R' = R'[q]/(h(f)), since R[q]/(f) is free of rank deg f; but R' ⊗_R R[q]^S → R'[q]^S need not be surjective even for flat R'. For R = ℤ, R' = ℚ and S = {1}, the element exp(q − 1) = Σ_k (q − 1)^k/k! of ℚ[q]^{1} = ℚ[[q − 1]] is not of the form x/m with x ∈ ℤ[[q − 1]] and m ≥ 1.

nodes.statement: For every sequence a_0, a_1, … ∈ R[q], with no degree condition, the series Σ_{n≥0} a_n(q) P_n(q) converges in R[q]^{ℕ>0}: its image in R[q]/(P_N) is the finite sum Σ_{n<N} a_n P_n, because P_N ∣ P_n for n ≥ N. More generally Σ_n b_n converges whenever b_n ∈ (P_{m_n}) with m_n → ∞. This defines an R[q]-linear map factorialSeries : R[q]^ℕ → R[q]^{ℕ>0}. It is surjective (HC.2/factorial-expansions) but not injective: (1 − q)·P_0 − 1·P_1 = 0. The Kontsevich series F = Σ_{n≥0} P_n (all a_n = 1) and Σ_n q^n P_n = q^{−1} (Habiro, Proposition 7.1) are elements; each is given by its compatible family of partial sums, never as a divergent formal expression.

nodes.title: The degree-normalised factorial expansion
nodes.statement: Every x ∈ R[q]^{ℕ>0} has a unique expansion x = Σ_{n≥0} a_n(q) P_n(q) with a_n ∈ R[q] and deg a_n ≤ n. The digits are computed by successive division with remainder by the monic polynomials q^{n+1} − 1 = −P_{n+1}/P_n. Starting from any representative r_0 ∈ R[q] of the image of x in R[q]/(P_N), put a_n = r_n mod (q^{n+1} − 1), of degree ≤ n, and r_{n+1} = (r_n − a_n)/(1 − q^{n+1}). Then r_0 = Σ_{n<N} a_n P_n + P_N r_N, and a_0, …, a_{N−1} depend only on the image of x in R[q]/(P_N). Uniqueness: (a_n)_{n<N} ↦ Σ a_n P_n is an isomorphism of R-modules ⊕_{n<N} R[q]_{≤n} → R[q]/(P_N), both free of rank N(N+1)/2. This is the case g_n = (−1)^n P_n of the source's unique expansion a = Σ a_n g_n with deg a_n < deg g_{n+1} − deg g_n along any cofinal chain of monic polynomials; for a general S the same holds along a chosen cofinal chain of Φ*_S. The division is not by P_N: P_N is not monic for odd N, and remainders modulo P_N have degree < N(N+1)/2 rather than the digit bound. Digit extraction commutes with ring maps. Unrestricted expansions are not unique: a_n may be changed by (1 − q^{n+1})c if a_{n+1} is changed by −c.
hypotheses: S = ℕ_{>0} for the factorial digits; for another S the digits are taken along a chosen cofinal chain of Φ*_S and depend on that choice.
Every commutative R: q^{n+1} − 1 is monic, so division with remainder and its uniqueness need no hypothesis on R.
Uniqueness holds only under deg a_n ≤ n.
proofSteps: Digits of a polynomial by the recursion above, with Polynomial.modByMonic and divByMonic by q^{n+1} − 1 (monic_X_pow_sub_C) and modByMonic_add_div.
Telescoping: r_0 = Σ_{n<N} a_n P_n + P_N r_N.
Independence of the representative: if P_N ∣ r_0 − r_0' then the first N digits agree, by induction on n with div_modByMonic_unique and cancellation of the non-zero-divisor P_n.

Uniqueness: two normalised expansions of the same element agree modulo P_1, P_2, … digit by digit (div_modByMonic_unique).
Compatibility with ring maps: Polynomial.map_modByMonic and map_divByMonic for the monic divisors.

nodes.title: Algorithms on normalised expansions, with congruence correctness
nodes.statement: Arithmetic on normalised expansions, each operation with a congruence correctness theorem modulo P_N. Addition and negation are digitwise, with no carries: the digits of x + y are a_n + b_n, since deg(a_n + b_n) ≤ n. Multiplication needs renormalisation: the n-th digit of xy is the n-th digit (HC.2/factorial-expansions) of the polynomial (Σ_{i≤n} a_i P_i)(Σ_{j≤n} b_j P_j). Carries propagate only towards higher indices, so digits 0, …, n of xy depend only on digits 0, …, n of x and y. Coefficient extraction computes digits 0, …, N − 1 of x from any polynomial representative of its image in R[q]/(P_N). Each operation has an executable version on integer coefficient lists, built on Tau Ceti's synthetic division (TauCeti.Polynomial.divModByMonicList, whose outputs are proved equal to Mathlib's /ₘ and %ₘ) and list multiplication, with a correctness theorem identifying it with the polynomial operation. Worked example, for the Kontsevich series F: F^2 ≡ 1 + (3 − q)P_1 + (6 − 3q − q^2)P_2 modulo P_3. The unrenormalised coefficient of P_2 is q^3 − q^2 − 3q + 5, of degree 3; it exceeds the digit by q^3 − 1 = −(1 − q^3), which is carried to index 3.
hypotheses: Inputs and outputs are normalised digit sequences.
Precision N means modulo P_N.
The executable versions work on descending coefficient lists, as in Tau Ceti's CoeffList.
proofSteps: Addition: Σ(a_n + b_n)P_n = Σ a_n P_n + Σ b_n P_n with deg(a_n + b_n) ≤ n; uniqueness of digits.
Multiplication: P_i P_j ∈ (P_{max(i,j)}), so modulo P_{n+1} only i, j ≤ n contribute; take digits of the product polynomial; correctness from the representative-independence of digits.
Finite dependence is read off the formula.

Executable versions: the digit recursion with divByMonicList and modByMonicList against the list of q^{n+1} − 1 below its leading coefficient, and mulCoeffList for products; correctness from ofCoeffList_divByMonicList, ofCoeffList_modByMonicList and ofCoeffList_mulCoeffList.
Worked examples: F^2 to precision 3, and q·q^{−1} = 1 to precision 3 (digits (1, 0, 0)).
acceptance: Addition is digitwise.

nodes.title: The indeterminate is invertible in every cyclotomic completion, and what may not be inverted
nodes.statement: For every S ⊆ ℕ_{>0} and every R, q is a unit of R[q]^S. Every f ∈ Φ*_S has constant term ±1 (Φ_1(0) = −1 and Φ_n(0) = 1 for n ≥ 2), so f = ±1 + q·g and q·(∓g) ≡ 1 modulo f; the inverses in the finite quotients are compatible (Habiro §7.1). For S = ℕ_{>0} the inverse is explicit: q^{−1} = Σ_{n≥0} q^n P_n (Habiro, Proposition 7.1). Its partial sums satisfy q·Σ_{n<N} q^n P_n = 1 − P_N, its normalised digits are q^n, and modulo P_3 it is 1 + q − q^3 − q^4 + q^5. Consequently, for every S and every f ∈ Φ*_S, R[q]/(f) → R[q, q^{−1}]/(f) is an isomorphism, and R[q]^S ≅ lim_{f∈Φ*_S} R[q, q^{−1}]/(f) as topological rings (stated by the source over ℤ). ι extends to R[q, q^{−1}] → R[q]^S, injective when S ≠ ∅. What may not be done: for n ∈ S with n > 0 and R ≠ 0, Φ_n is not a unit of R[q]^S, so no formal division by it exists, and R[q]^S is not a field. The unit group is not determined here: Habiro's Conjecture 7.1, U(ℤ[q]^{ℕ>0}) = {±q^i}, is open and is not used; for other S the unit group can be larger (Remark 7.1: for odd m ≥ 3 the alternating sum Σ_{i<m} (−1)^i q^i is a unit of ℤ[q]^S for S = {n : gcd(n, 2m) = 1}).
hypotheses: Any R and any S. The earlier hypothesis that S must contain 1 is false: for S = {2}, ℤ[q]^{2} = ℤ[[q + 1]] and q = −1 + (q + 1) is a unit.
The non-unit statement needs R ≠ 0 and n ∈ S with n > 0.
Conjecture 7.1 is open and is recorded only as such.
proofSteps: Constant terms: Φ_1 = q − 1 (cyclotomic_one) and cyclotomic_coeff_zero for n ≥ 2; products have constant term ±1.
q is a unit in every R[q]/(f), and inverses are unique, hence compatible; so q is a unit in the limit.
Proposition 7.1: q·Σ_{n<N} q^n P_n = Σ_{n<N} (P_n − P_{n+1}) = 1 − P_N (the source's telescoping proof, p. 1142); take the factorial series of HC.2/factorial-series.
Laurent comparison: since q is a unit in R[q]/(f), the localisation map R[q]/(f) → R[q, q^{−1}]/(f) is an isomorphism (LaurentPolynomial.isLocalization, IsLocalization.Away.lift); pass to the limit.
Non-units: HC.1/the-cyclotomic-completion.
Remark 7.1 as an example of a larger unit group, with the corrected argument of source issue E4.
acceptance: q is a unit of R[q]^S for every S, including S = {2}.
q·Σ_{n<N} q^n P_n = 1 − P_N; q^{−1} ≡ 1 + q − q^3 − q^4 + q^5 modulo P_3.
R[q]^S ≅ lim_{f∈Φ*_S} R[q, q^{−1}]/(f) for every S.
Φ_n (n ∈ S, n > 0) is not a unit when R ≠ 0, and Conjecture 7.1 is not used.

nodes.title: Evaluation at a root of unity
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, S a set of positive integers, n in S, and zeta an element of an R-algebra A with Phi_n(zeta) = 0 (in a domain of characteristic zero this holds exactly for the primitive n-th roots of unity). EVALUATION at zeta is the R-algebra map ev_zeta : R[q]^S -> A obtained by composing the projection R[q]^S -> R[q]/(Phi_n) = AdjoinRoot Phi_n with the map AdjoinRoot Phi_n -> A sending the class of q to zeta. It is independent of the truncation: for every f in Phi_S^* divisible by Phi_n and every polynomial g representing the image of x in R[q]/(f), ev_zeta(x) = g(zeta); on the image of R[q] it is ordinary evaluation. For S = N and zeta primitive of order m in a domain, ev_zeta(sum_k a_k(q)(q;q)_k) = sum_{k<m} a_k(zeta)(zeta;zeta)_k. For R = Z and S = N the evaluations at all roots of unity in C assemble into Habiro's map epsilon : Z[q]^N -> Map(Z_N, Z[Z_N]). Only roots of the Phi_m, m in S, are points: a continuous ring map from R[q]^S to a discrete domain factors through some R[q]/(f), f in Phi_S^*, so it sends q to a root of some Phi_m with m in S; for instance no ring homomorphism Z[q]^{1} = Z[[q-1]] -> Z sends q to -1, because 2 - q is a unit of Z[[q-1]] and would map to 3.
hypotheses: n lies in S and zeta is an element of an R-algebra A with Phi_n(zeta) = 0. In a domain of characteristic zero this is equivalent to zeta being a primitive n-th root of unity (IsPrimitiveRoot.isRoot_cyclotomic, Polynomial.isRoot_cyclotomic_iff); in a general ring a primitive root need not be a root of Phi_n (in Z/8Z, 3 is a primitive square root of 1 but Phi_2(3) = 4), so the hypothesis is Phi_n(zeta) = 0.

The canonical target is AdjoinRoot Phi_n = R[q]/(Phi_n); Habiro's R[zeta] is its image under q -> zeta. The map AdjoinRoot Phi_n -> R[zeta] is an isomorphism when Phi_n is irreducible over the fraction field of R (R = Z: cyclotomic.irreducible_rat), not merely irreducible in R[q]: for R = Z[2i] and n = 4, q^2 + 1 is irreducible in R[q] but the nonzero class of 2 + 2i q maps to 0 in R[i] = Z[i].
Independence of the truncation is part of the construction; it uses only that the projections of HC.1 are compatible.
proofSteps: Phi_n lies in Phi_S^* because n is in S, so the projection R[q]^S -> R[q]/(Phi_n) exists (HC.1/the-cyclotomic-completion).
AdjoinRoot.liftAlgHom Phi_n zeta exists because Phi_n(zeta) = 0; define ev_zeta as its composite with the projection.
If Phi_n divides f and g represents x modulo f, the projection of x to R[q]/(Phi_n) is the class of g by compatibility of the projections, so ev_zeta(x) = g(zeta).
On polynomials ev_zeta(fromPoly g) = aeval zeta g, by construction.

For S = N and zeta primitive of order m in a domain, (zeta;zeta)_k = 0 for k >= m, and a factorial series converges in the completion (HC.2/factorial-expansions); continuity of ev_zeta for the discrete topology on A gives the finite sum.

Continuous maps to discrete domains: the kernel is open, so it contains the kernel of some projection to R[q]/(f), f = prod Phi_m^{k_m}; f(phi(q)) = 0 in a domain forces Phi_m(phi(q)) = 0 for some m in S. For S = {1}, 2 - q = 1 - (q - 1) is a unit of Z[[q-1]].
Assemble epsilon for R = Z, S = N (Habiro, p. 1128).
acceptance: ev_zeta(x) = g(zeta) for every representative g of x modulo any f in Phi_S^* divisible by Phi_n.
ev_zeta is an R-algebra homomorphism extending aeval zeta on R[q].
For the Kontsevich series F = sum_k (q;q)_k over Z: ev_1 F = 1, ev_{-1} F = 3, ev_{zeta_3} F = 5 - zeta_3, ev_i F = 8 - 3i (PARI).
There is no ring homomorphism Z[[q-1]] -> Z sending q to -1.
The completion at the empty set is the zero ring and has no evaluation into a nonzero ring.

nodes.title: The Taylor map at a root of unity
nodes.statement: For n in S and zeta in an R-algebra A with Phi_n(zeta) = 0, the TAYLOR MAP (Habiro's expansion homomorphism sigma_zeta) is the R-algebra map sigma_zeta : R[q]^S -> A[[X]], X standing for q - zeta, whose k-th coefficient on x is (D_k g)(zeta) for any polynomial g representing x modulo any f in Phi_S^* divisible by Phi_n^{k+1}, where D_k is the k-th Hasse derivative (for x = fromPoly g this is Mathlib's Polynomial.taylor_coeff). It is well defined because (q - zeta)^{k+1} divides Phi_n(q)^{k+1} in A[q], and multiplicative because the polynomial Taylor shift is an algebra map. Its constant coefficient is ev_zeta. The comparison with ordinary derivatives is k! * (coefficient k) = (d/dq)^k g (zeta) (Polynomial.factorial_smul_hasseDeriv); D_1 is the derivative itself. Over a torsion-free ring such as Z[zeta] this determines the coefficient (the division by k! is exact); over a ring where k! is a zero-divisor it does not: over F_2 the second Taylor coefficient of q^2 at 1 is 1 while its second derivative is 0. For the Kontsevich series F over Z, sigma_1(F) = 1 - X + 2X^2 - 5X^3 + 15X^4 - 53X^5 + 217X^6 - 1014X^7 + O(X^8) (signed Fishburn numbers) and sigma_{-1}(F) = 3 + 11X + 72X^2 + 635X^3 + 7085X^4 + O(X^5).
hypotheses: n lies in S and Phi_n(zeta) = 0 in the R-algebra A; the target is A[[X]] with X = q - zeta. Habiro's sigma_zeta is the case A = R[zeta] inside an algebraic closure of the fraction field of a domain R.
The k-th coefficient is computed from any representative modulo an element of Phi_S^* divisible by Phi_n^{k+1}.
k! * D_k = (d/dq)^k; this determines D_k only where k! is a non-zero-divisor. D_1 is the ordinary derivative (hasseDeriv_one).
proofSteps: (q - zeta) divides Phi_n(q) in A[q] because Phi_n(zeta) = 0, hence (q - zeta)^{k+1} | Phi_n^{k+1} | f.
If h in A[q] is divisible by (q - zeta)^{k+1}, then taylor zeta h is divisible by X^{k+1}, so (D_j h)(zeta) = 0 for j <= k; hence the k-th coefficient does not depend on the representative.
Define sigma_zeta(x) = PowerSeries.mk (k -> (D_k g_k)(zeta)); additivity and multiplicativity hold coefficientwise because Polynomial.taylorAlgHom zeta is an algebra map.
The constant coefficient is D_0 g (zeta) = g(zeta) = ev_zeta(x).
On fromPoly g, sigma_zeta is the coercion of taylor zeta g (Polynomial.taylor_coeff).
k! * coeff_k = (d/dq)^k g (zeta) by Polynomial.factorial_smul_hasseDeriv; the F_2 example shows that the coefficient is not a function of the derivatives when 2 = 0.
Record the Kontsevich expansions at 1 and -1 (PARI) and the source's description of sigma_zeta as the power series expansion at zeta.

k! * coeff_k (sigma_zeta x) = (d/dq)^k g (zeta); over F_2 the second Taylor coefficient of q^2 at 1 is 1 although the second derivative is 0.

nodes.title: Naturality of evaluation and the Taylor map
nodes.statement: Evaluation and the Taylor map are natural in four ways. (1) Coefficients: for a ring map h : R -> R' and compatible algebra maps A -> A', ev_{h(zeta)} o h^S = h_A o ev_zeta and sigma_{h(zeta)} o h^S = PowerSeries.map h_A o sigma_zeta, where h^S is HC.1's coefficient map. nodes.title: Which roots of unity are p-adically close
nodes.statement: Let B be a commutative ring and p a prime. (a) If omega in B satisfies omega^{p^e} = 1, then (omega - 1)^{p^e} lies in pB; hence for roots of unity zeta, zeta' in B with (zeta^{-1} zeta')^{p^e} = 1, (zeta' - zeta)^{p^e} lies in pB and zeta' - zeta is topologically nilpotent for the p-adic topology. (b) If omega is a root of Phi_m with m > 1 not a prime power, then 1 - omega is a unit of B; so two roots of unity whose ratio has order > 1 and not a prime power differ by a unit, which is topologically nilpotent in no nonzero separated ring. Hence in a domain of characteristic zero two roots of unity are p-adically close exactly when their ratio has p-power order; orders differing by a power of p is NOT enough: e^{2 pi i/6} - e^{2 pi i/3} = 1, whereas e^{2 pi i/6} = -e^{4 pi i/3} is 2-adically close to e^{4 pi i/3}. Every root of order m p^k is p-adically close to a root of order m (for p not dividing m, the one with the same prime-to-p part); this is why GSWZ fix a compatible collection (zeta_m) with zeta_{mm'} = zeta_m zeta_{m'} for coprime m, m' and zeta_{p^r}^p = zeta_{p^{r-1}}, for which v_p(zeta_{pm} - zeta_m) > 0.

nodes.title: The p-adic re-expansion of power series
nodes.statement: Let B be a commutative ring that is p-adically complete and separated, and c in B with c^N in pB for some N. RE-EXPANSION by c is the continuous ring homomorphism rex_c : B[[X]] -> B[[X]], f(X) -> f(X + c), defined as PowerSeries.eval2Hom of the constant embedding at the point X + C c, which is topologically nilpotent for the product topology on B[[X]] over the p-adic topology of B. Its j-th coefficient on f = sum a_k X^k is the p-adically convergent sum sum_{k>=j} binom(k,j) c^{k-j} a_k. On polynomials rex_c is Polynomial.taylor c; rex_0 = id; and the COCYCLE LAW rex_{c'} o rex_c = rex_{c+c'} holds, so rex_c is an automorphism with inverse rex_{-c}. Mathlib's PowerSeries.subst cannot be used here: its hypothesis is that the constant coefficient of the substituted series is NILPOTENT, and a nonzero constant c in a domain never is. In the source this is the isomorphism rho_{(fg),(f)} for f = X - c', g = X - c over an adically complete ring (first half of the proof of Proposition 3.1); in GSWZ it is the re-expansion after shifting x to x + zeta_pm - zeta_m.
hypotheses: B is p-adically complete and separated; B[[X]] carries the product topology of the p-adic topology on coefficients (complete and Hausdorff by IsAdic.isAdicComplete_iff and the Pi-topology instances).
c^N lies in pB for some N; by HC.3/p-adic-closeness-of-roots this holds for c = zeta' - zeta when zeta^{-1} zeta' has p-power order.
Without completeness of B the defining sums need not converge: for B = Z, c = -2 and f = sum X^k the constant term would be sum (-2)^k.
proofSteps: HasEval (X + C c): X is topologically nilpotent in the product topology, C c is because c^N lies in pB, and HasEval is stable under addition in a linearly topologised ring (HasEval.add).
Define rex_c := PowerSeries.eval2Hom (continuity of C) (HasEval (X + C c)); the coefficient formula follows from hasSum_eval2.
On polynomials eval2 is Polynomial.eval2 (eval2_coe), i.e. Polynomial.taylor c.
Cocycle: rex_{c'} o rex_c and rex_{c+c'} are continuous and agree on polynomials by Polynomial.taylor_taylor, hence agree (eval2_unique).
Record the non-example: re-expansion across a unit difference is undefined.
acceptance: rex_c(g) = taylor c g for polynomials g.
rex_0 = id and rex_{c'} o rex_c = rex_{c+c'}.
In Z_2[[X]], rex_{-2}(sum_k X^k) = 1/(3 - X) has constant coefficient 1/3.

nodes.title: Adjacency of cyclotomic orders and connectedness
nodes.statement: For positive integers m, n let c_{m,n} = 0 if m = n; c_{m,n} = p if n/m = p^j for a prime p and an integer j != 0; c_{m,n} = 1 otherwise (Habiro, p. 1134). For a ring R, m and n are ADJACENT over R, written m <=>_R n, when R is c_{m,n}-adically separated, i.e. the intersection of the ideals c_{m,n}^j R is zero (Mathlib: IsHausdorff (span {c_{m,n}}) R). Thus m <=>_R m for every R; for m != n and R != 0, m <=>_R n iff n/m = p^{+-k} with k >= 1 and R p-adically separated. The relation is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive (over Z: 1 <=> 2 <=> 6 but not 1 <=> 6). A set S of orders is CONNECTED over R when it is non-empty and any two of its elements are joined by a chain of adjacent elements lying in S (chains of length 0 allowed). The set of divisors of n is connected over R iff R is p-adically separated for every prime p dividing n.
hypotheses: R is commutative and unital. Habiro assumes R != 0; for R = 0 every ideal is separated, all orders are adjacent and every completion is zero, so allowing it changes nothing.
p-adic separatedness refers to the ideal pR generated by the integer p, which need not be a prime ideal of R.
Over Q, and over any ring in which every prime is a unit, m <=> n iff m = n. Over Z, and over every subring of the algebraic integers, m <=> n iff m = n or n/m is a non-trivial power of a prime.
proofSteps: Define c_{m,n} and adjacency through IsHausdorff; reflexivity is IsHausdorff for the zero ideal; symmetry because c_{m,n} = c_{n,m}.
For m != n with a ratio that is not a prime power, c = 1, and IsHausdorff for the unit ideal forces R = 0 (IsHausdorff.subsingleton).
Over Q the ideal pQ = Q is not separated; over Z every pZ is; a subring of the algebraic integers is p-separated because x/p^j integral for all j forces the norm of x to vanish.

Divisors of n: if R is p-separated for all p | n, join each divisor to 1 by removing one prime factor at a time; if R is not p-separated for some p | n, every edge preserves the p-adic valuation, so 1 and p lie in different components.
Non-transitivity over Z: 1 <=> 2 and 2 <=> 6, but 6 is not a prime power.
acceptance: m <=>_R m for every ring R, including R = Q.
Over Z, m <=> n iff m = n or n/m = p^{+-k} with k >= 1.
Over Q, m <=> n iff m = n, so the connected sets over Q are the singletons.
The divisors of 12 form a connected set over Z but not over Z[1/3] (1 and 3 lie in different components).

nodes.title: The radical relation between monic polynomials
nodes.statement: For a ring R, an ideal I and monic f, g in R[q], write f =>^I_R g if f lies in the radical of (g) + I[q], i.e. f^m lies in (g) + I[q] for some m; write f =>_R g if f =>^I_R g for some ideal I with R I-adically separated. For M' subset M of monic polynomials write M' < M if every f in M is reached from an element of M' by a chain f_0 => f_1 => ... => f_r = f inside M. The ideal I can always be taken finitely generated: replace it by the ideal generated by the coefficients of f^m - g h, which lie in I; R remains separated for the smaller ideal.
hypotheses: f and g are monic.
Separatedness is IsHausdorff I R.
proofSteps: Define the relations.
g | f implies f => g (take I = 0).
f => g, f | f' and g' | g imply f' => g'.
Finitely generated I: the coefficients of f^m - g h generate J subset I, f^m lies in (g) + J[q], and the intersection of the J^j is inside that of the I^j.
acceptance: Phi_2 =>_Z Phi_1 with I = (2), since Phi_2 = Phi_1 + 2.
Phi_2 does not =>_Q Phi_1: evaluating Phi_2^m = Phi_1 h + i(q) at q = 1 gives 2^m in I, so I = Q, which is not separated.

nodes.title: One-step injectivity for monic completions
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring and f, g monic with f =>_R g. Then the restriction rho_{(fg),(f)} : R[q]^{(fg)} -> R[q]^{(f)} from the (fg)-adic to the f-adic completion of R[q] is injective. If moreover R is I-adically complete for a finitely generated ideal I with f =>^I g, the map is an isomorphism (this isomorphism, for f = q - zeta', g = q - zeta, is the source form of re-expansion).
hypotheses: f and g are monic.
The ideal I witnessing f =>_R g is taken finitely generated (HC.4/radical-relation-on-monic-polynomials); the source's proof needs this, see the source issues.
proofSteps: Complete case: for R I-adically complete, R[q]^{(f)} = R[q]^{(f)+I[q]} and R[q]^{(fg)} = R[q]^{(fg)+I[q]}; since ((f) + I[q])^m is inside (fg) + I[q], which is inside (f) + I[q], the two topologies coincide and rho is an isomorphism.

General case: R -> R^_I is injective (AdicCompletion.of_injective) and, I being finitely generated, R^_I is I-adically complete (AdicCompletion.isAdicComplete); the vertical maps of the square are injective by HC.1/coefficient-change-injective-and-surjective and the bottom map is an isomorphism, so the top map is injective.
acceptance: Over Z, Z[q]^{(q^2-1)} -> Z[[q-1]] is injective (f = Phi_1, g = Phi_2, I = (2)).
Over Z_2 the same map is an isomorphism.
Over Q it is not injective (it kills the idempotent of the (q+1)-factor), and indeed Phi_1 does not =>_Q Phi_2.

In particular, if M is =>_R-connected (non-empty, any two elements joined by a chain of => inside M), then rho_{M,M'} is injective for every non-empty M' subset M (Corollary 3.1).

Lemma 3.2: the finite extensions M' of M_0 with M_0 < M' are cofinal (add the finitely many chains).
Reduce to M minus M_0 = {g}.
M_0 finite: with f the product of M_0, some element of M_0 => g, so f => g, and one-step injectivity applies.
M_0 infinite: write both completions as limits over finite U containing some g_0 => g, apply the finite case to U < U + {g}, and use that limits preserve injectivity.

nodes.statement: (1) For all m, n and every ring R, Phi_m(q) lies in the radical of (Phi_n(q), c_{m,n}) in R[q], i.e. Phi_m =>^{(c_{m,n})}_R Phi_n. (2) For R != 0, m <=>_R n iff Phi_m =>_R Phi_n. Hence S is connected over R iff Phi_S is =>_R-connected, and the chain hypothesis of Theorem 4.1 for S' subset S is Phi_{S'} < Phi_S.
hypotheses: Adjacency is the corrected relation of HC.4/adjacency-of-orders, reflexive by the c_{n,n} = 0 clause; without that clause (2) fails for m = n over Q.
proofSteps: c = 0: m = n, trivial. c = p and m = p^e n: Phi_m = Phi_n^d modulo p, so Phi_m lies in (Phi_n) + pR[q]. c = p and n = p^e m: Phi_n = Phi_m^d modulo p, so Phi_m^d lies in (Phi_n) + pR[q]; this is where the radical is needed. c = 1: (Phi_m, Phi_n) = (1).
(2), only if: from (1) with I = (c_{m,n}).

(2), if: if Phi_m^i lies in (Phi_n) + I[q] with R I-separated and c = p, then p^i lies in (Phi_n) + I[q] by (4.2), hence in I because Phi_n is monic and R[q]/(Phi_n) is R-free on a basis containing 1; so R is p-separated. If c = 1 then 1 lies in I and R = 0.

nodes.title: Injectivity of the restriction maps along a connected chain
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring and S' subset S sets of orders such that every n in S is joined to some n' in S' by a chain n' <=>_R ... <=>_R n of adjacent orders lying in S. Then rho_{S,S'} : R[q]^S -> R[q]^{S'} is INJECTIVE (Habiro, Theorem 4.1). In particular, if S is connected over R then rho_{S,S'} is injective for every non-empty S' subset S; and rho_{N,S'} : Z[q]^N -> Z[q]^{S'} is injective for every non-empty S'; for m | n, rho_{<n>,<m>} is injective over Z, so Z[q]^N is the intersection of the Z[q]^{<n>} inside Z[[q-1]] (Corollary 4.1). The chains must lie in S: over Z the order 6 is joined to 1 through 2 in N, yet rho_{{1,6},{1}} : Z[q]^{{1,6}} -> Z[[q-1]] is not injective, since (Phi_1, Phi_6) = (1) makes Z[q]^{{1,6}} the product Z[[q-1]] x Z[q]^{6}. The conclusion is injectivity only; non-surjectivity is HC.4/non-surjectivity.
hypotheses: The chain hypothesis is as stated: for each element of the larger set there is a chain of adjacent elements inside the larger set ending in the smaller set.
Adjacency is over the coefficient ring, so the hypothesis involves the separatedness of that ring at the relevant primes.
The conclusion is injectivity of the restriction, not surjectivity; non-surjectivity is a later node.
proofSteps: Identify R[q]^S with the monic completion R[q]^{Phi_S} (HC.1).
By HC.4/adjacency-is-the-radical-relation, the chain hypothesis for S' subset S is exactly Phi_{S'} precedes Phi_S in the sense of HC.4/radical-relation-on-monic-polynomials.
Apply HC.4/chain-injectivity-for-monic-completions (Habiro Theorem 3.1).
Corollaries: a connected S satisfies the hypothesis for every non-empty S'; N and every divisor set <m> are connected over Z.

Non-example: Phi_6 - q Phi_1 = 1, so Phi_1^k and Phi_6^k are comaximal and the Chinese remainder theorem (Ideal.quotientInfRingEquivPiQuotient) splits every finite level; the element (0, 1) of Z[[q-1]] x Z[q]^{6} is nonzero and killed by rho_{{1,6},{1}}.
acceptance: If S is connected over R, rho_{S,S'} is injective for every non-empty S' subset S.
Over Z, rho_{N,S'} is injective for every non-empty S'.
rho_{{1,6},{1}} is not injective over Z although 1 <=> 2 <=> 6 in N: the chain leaves S = {1, 6}.
For m | n, rho_{<n>,<m>} is injective over Z (Corollary 4.1).

nodes.title: Adjacency of roots of unity and connectedness of the primitive roots
nodes.statement: Let R be an integral domain of characteristic 0 with roots of unity Z^R. For zeta, zeta' in Z^R put zeta <=>_R zeta' when zeta = zeta', or ord(zeta^{-1} zeta') = p^k with k >= 1 and R p-adically separated; this is equivalent to (q - zeta) =>_R (q - zeta') and to R being (zeta - zeta')-adically separated (Habiro Lemma 5.1, with the zeta = zeta' case made explicit). Theorem 5.1: if Z subset Z^R is <=>_R-connected then rho_{Z,Z'} : R[q]^Z -> R[q]^{Z'} is injective for every non-empty Z' subset Z, R[q]^Z being the monic completion at the q - zeta, zeta in Z. Step of Theorem 5.2: if all primitive n-th roots lie in R, R is p-separated for every odd p | n and 2-separated when 4 | n, then the set Z_n of primitive n-th roots is <=>_R-connected.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain of characteristic 0 containing the roots considered.
For Z_n: the separation hypotheses of Theorem 5.2.
proofSteps: Lemma 5.1: (1) implies (2) by evaluating (q - zeta)^m in (q - zeta') + I[q] at zeta'; (2) implies (1) with I = (zeta - zeta'); (2) iff (3) by HC.3/p-adic-closeness-of-roots: for ratio of order p^k the ideals (zeta - zeta') and (p) define the same topology, otherwise zeta - zeta' is a unit and R != 0.
Theorem 5.1 is Corollary 3.1 (HC.4/chain-injectivity-for-monic-completions) for M = {q - zeta : zeta in Z}.

Z_n is the product of the Z_{p_i^{e_i}} under multiplication; change one coordinate at a time; the ratio of two elements of Z_{p^e} has p-power order; Z_2 = {-1} is a singleton, so p = 2 with e = 1 needs no hypothesis.

Z_3 inside Z[zeta_3, 1/3] is not connected: zeta_3 - zeta_3^2 is a unit.
Z_6 inside Z[zeta_3, 1/2] is connected: the Z_2 factor is {-1} and Z[zeta_3, 1/2] is 3-separated.

nodes.title: A single Taylor expansion determines the element
nodes.statement: For an integral domain of characteristic zero, a connected set of orders and an order in it, if the ring is separated at each odd prime factor of that order and also at two when four divides it, then the Taylor map at a primitive root of that order is INJECTIVE. In particular over the integers, with all orders, the Taylor expansion at any single root of unity determines the element completely. The hypotheses are the source's and are carried here: a domain of characteristic zero, connectedness, and the separation conditions with their asymmetry between odd primes and the prime two.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain of characteristic 0; zeta is a primitive n-th root of unity in an algebraic closure of the fraction field of R, possibly outside R; the target is R[zeta][[q - zeta]].

R is p-adically separated for every odd prime p | n, and 2-adically separated if 4 | n. These are sufficient, not necessary (for R = Z[1/2], S = {4}, sigma_i is still injective by Galois symmetry), but neither can be dropped in general: see the acceptance lines.
S is connected over R and contains n.

The reduction to zeta in R needs the hypotheses for R[zeta]; for Noetherian R they transfer (Krull's intersection theorem for the Noetherian domain R[zeta], and p stays a non-unit in an integral extension). The source does not check this (see the source issues); every ring the atlas uses (Z, Z[1/N], rings of integers) is Noetherian.
proofSteps: R -> R[zeta] is injective, so R[q]^S -> R[zeta][q]^S is injective (HC.1/coefficient-change-injective-and-surjective, Habiro Lemma 3.1).
With zeta in R: sigma_zeta = rho_{{n},(q-zeta)} o rho_{S,{n}}, and rho_{S,{n}} is injective by Theorem 4.1 (HC.4/injectivity-of-restriction).

Phi_n = prod over primitive n-th roots xi of (q - xi) in R[q], so R[q]^{n} = R[q]^{Z_n}; by HC.4/connectedness-of-primitive-roots the set Z_n is connected under the separation hypotheses, and Theorem 5.1 makes rho_{Z_n,{zeta}} injective.
Integral corollary: Z is p-separated for every p and N is connected over Z, so sigma_zeta is injective on Z[q]^N for every root of unity zeta.
Vogel obtained the case zeta = 1 independently (source, p. 1135).
acceptance: Over Z with S = N, sigma_zeta is injective for every root of unity zeta.

The 2-adic hypothesis matters only when 4 | n: for R = Z[1/2] and S = {2}, sigma_{-1} is the identity of Z[1/2][[q+1]]; for R = Z[i, 1/2] and S = {4}, sigma_i is not injective, since q - i and q + i are comaximal (2i is a unit) and R[q]^{4} = R[[q-i]] x R[[q+i]].
At an odd prime: for R = Z[zeta_3, 1/3] and S = {3}, sigma_{zeta_3} is not injective (zeta_3 - zeta_3^2 is a unit).
Over Q with S = N (or any S containing ord zeta with at least two elements) sigma_zeta is not injective; this is proved in HC.5 (Habiro §7.5), not here. For S = {n} over Q it is injective.
Injectivity only: over Z, sigma_zeta is never surjective (HC.4/taylor-maps-are-not-surjective).

A subring of a domain is a domain.

nodes.title: Evaluation uniqueness, with the precise infinite-set condition
nodes.statement: Let R be a subring of the algebraic numbers, S a set of orders connected over R and T subset S. Write P_T(R) = prod_{n in T} R[q]/(Phi_n(q)) and epsilon_{S,T} : R[q]^S -> P_T(R) for the map given by reduction modulo each Phi_n, n in T (equivalently, evaluation at all primitive n-th roots of unity, n in T). If for SOME n in S infinitely many m in T satisfy m <=>_R n, then epsilon_{S,T} is injective (Habiro, Theorem 6.1). In particular, if R is contained in the algebraic integers and T contains infinitely many prime powers, epsilon_{N,T} : R[q]^N -> P_T(R) is injective. A finite T never suffices: prod_{n in T} Phi_n is a nonzero element of the kernel. The hypothesis couples infinitude with adjacency to one order: an infinite T without it, such as T = {6, 15, 35, 77, ...} (products of consecutive primes, each order n being adjacent to at most two of them), is simply not covered, and whether epsilon_{N,T} is injective for such T is OPEN; Habiro conjectures (Conjecture 6.1) that over Z evaluation on ANY infinite set of roots of unity is injective. No non-injectivity statement for infinite sets is available. The version for individual roots is HC.4/evaluation-at-individual-roots.
hypotheses: R is a subring of the algebraic numbers (the last step of the proof uses that its elements are algebraic); for the corollary R lies in the algebraic integers, which makes R p-separated for every p and N connected over R.
The condition is on one order n in S with infinitely many adjacent m in T, not on the size of T.
S is connected over R.
proofSteps: Suppose a != 0 with epsilon_{S,T}(a) = 0; rho_{S,{n}}(a) != 0 by Theorem 4.1; write rho_{S,{n}}(a) = sum_{j>=l} a_j Phi_n^j with a_l not in (Phi_n).
Choose infinitely many distinct m_i in T with m_i <=> n and n | m_i, so m_i/n = p_i^{e_i} with R p_i-separated.

Phi_{m_i} divides a in R[q]^S (HC.1/the-quotients-of-the-completion). By induction Phi_{m_1}...Phi_{m_k} | a: from (6.1), b(xi) = 0 for EVERY primitive m_k-th root xi because Phi_{m_j}(xi) != 0 for j < k, hence Phi_{m_k} | b in R[q].

By (4.1), Phi_{m_1}...Phi_{m_k} lies in (p_1...p_k, Phi_n); its reduction modulo Phi_n is a non-zero-divisor of R[q]/(Phi_n) (it vanishes at no primitive n-th root), so comparing lowest Phi_n-adic terms gives p_1...p_k | abar_l in R[q]/(Phi_n) = R^{phi(n)}.

A nonzero x in R subset Qbar has x/p in R for only finitely many primes p with 1/p not in R (p must divide the constant term of an integral equation of x); so some prime p occurs infinitely often among the p_i, x lies in the intersection of the p^j R, which is 0; hence abar_l = 0, a contradiction.
Corollary: over subrings of the algebraic integers every prime power is adjacent to 1 and N is connected.
Record Conjecture 6.1 and the non-example T = {6, 15, 35, 77, ...}.
acceptance: Over Z, epsilon_{N,N} is injective, and so is epsilon_{N,T} for T = {2^k : k >= 1}.
For finite T, prod_{n in T} Phi_n is a nonzero element of ker epsilon_{S,T}.
Theorem 6.1 says nothing about T = {6, 15, 35, 77, ...}; Habiro's Conjecture 6.1 predicts injectivity there, so no failure of injectivity for infinite sets may be asserted.
Over Z the completion embeds in P_N(Z) = prod_n Z[q]/(Phi_n).

nodes.title: Evaluation at individual roots determines the element
nodes.statement: Let R be a subring of the algebraic numbers, S a set of orders connected over R, and Z a set of roots of unity with orders in S such that Phi_{ord zeta} is irreducible over the fraction field of R for every zeta in Z (for instance R = Z). If for some n in S infinitely many zeta in Z have ord zeta <=>_R n, then epsilon_{S,Z} : R[q]^S -> prod_{zeta in Z} R[zeta], x -> (ev_zeta x), is injective. In particular, over Z with S = N, an element vanishing at infinitely many roots of unity of prime-power order is zero, and epsilon : Z[q]^N -> Map(Z_N, Z[Z_N]) is injective (Habiro, Theorem 6.2 and p. 1128). Habiro states Theorem 6.2 for every subring of the algebraic numbers, but the printed proof uses that R[q]/(Phi_n) -> prod_{zeta in Z, ord zeta = n} R[zeta] is injective, which fails when Phi_n splits over the fraction field of R and Z misses a factor (R = Z[i], n = 4, Z meeting the primitive 4th roots in {i}: the class of q - i is killed); the irreducibility hypothesis restores the proof, and covers every use in the atlas.

nodes.title: The injective maps are not isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Over Z (Habiro, Proposition 7.4): (1) if m <=>_Z n and m != n, rho_{{m,n},{m}} : Z[q]^{{m,n}} -> Z[q]^{m} is not surjective; (2) if m | n and m != n, rho_{<n>,<m>} : Z[q]^{<n>} -> Z[q]^{<m>} is not surjective; (3) for every non-empty finite S, rho_{N,S} : Z[q]^N -> Z[q]^S is not surjective. Since these maps are injective (Theorem 4.1), they are proper embeddings, never identifications. Over Q, by contrast, restriction maps are surjective (Habiro §7.5), so non-surjectivity is an integral phenomenon. The Taylor maps are treated in HC.4/taylor-maps-are-not-surjective, because §7.4 of the source says nothing about them.
hypotheses: The coefficient ring is Z throughout.
The three statements concern restriction maps only.
(1) uses (4.1)-(4.2) and the p-adic integers; (2) uses the finite free base change Z[q^m] -> Z[q]; (3) uses (2) and Theorem 4.1.
proofSteps: (1): m/n = p^e with e != 0. The map b : Z[q]^{m} -> Z_p[q]/(Phi_n) = lim_j Z[q]/(Phi_n, p^j) is well defined and surjective because Phi_m lies in (Phi_n, p) and p lies in (Phi_m, Phi_n) (HC.4/cyclotomic-congruence-and-prime-ideal); with c : Z[q]/(Phi_n) -> Z_p[q]/(Phi_n) the square commutes, and c is not surjective because Z -> Z_p is not and Z[q]/(Phi_n) is free; hence rho is not surjective. Witness for {1, 2}: 1/(2 - q) = sum_k (q-1)^k maps to 1/3 in Z_2.

(2): for a prime p | n/m the image of rho_{,} lies in the image of rho_{,}, so reduce to n = pm. Z[q] is free of rank m over Z[q^m] and adic completion commutes with finite free base change (AdicCompletion.ofTensorProductEquivOfPiFintype), so rho_{,} is m copies of rho_{

,<1>} over Z[q^m], which is case (1) for {1, p}.

(3): with m = lcm(S) and n = 2m, rho_{N,S} = rho_{<m>,S} o rho_{<n>,<m>} o rho_{N,<n>}; the middle map is not surjective by (2) and rho_{<m>,S} is injective by Theorem 4.1 (<m> is connected over Z), so an element of Z[q]^{<m>} outside the middle image maps outside the image of rho_{N,S}.

nodes.title: The Taylor maps are not surjective
nodes.statement: For every root of unity zeta in C, sigma_zeta : Z[q]^N -> Z[zeta][[q - zeta]] is injective (Theorem 5.2) but not surjective. If ord zeta = n >= 2, the unit 1/(1 + Phi_n(q)) of Z[zeta][[q - zeta]] (constant term 1) is not in the image; if zeta = 1, 1/(2 - q) is not. For ord zeta >= 3 the image already misses q - zeta modulo (q - zeta)^2, because Phi_n'(zeta) is not a unit (|disc Phi_n| > 1). The source asserts this non-surjectivity in its introduction but its §7.4 treats only restriction maps, which covers ord zeta in {1, 2}, where sigma_zeta = rho_{N,{ord zeta}}. Over Q, by contrast, sigma_zeta is surjective: Q[q]^N is the product of the Q[q]^{n} (Habiro §7.5), and sigma_zeta restricted to Q[q]^{n} is an isomorphism onto Q(zeta)[[q - zeta]] (a map of complete discrete valuation rings that is an isomorphism on residue fields and sends the uniformiser Phi_n to Phi_n'(zeta)(q - zeta) + ..., with Phi_n'(zeta) != 0).
hypotheses: The coefficient ring is Z and S = N.
zeta is a root of unity of order n.
proofSteps: g = 1 + Phi_n (n >= 2) or g = 2 - q (n = 1) is a unit of Z[zeta][[q - zeta]] because ev_zeta(g) = 1.
If sigma_zeta(a) = 1/g, then sigma_zeta(g a - 1) = 0, so g a = 1 by injectivity, and ev_xi(g) would be a unit of Z[xi] for every root xi.
But ev_1(1 + Phi_n) = 1 + Phi_n(1) is 2 if n is not a prime power and 1 + p if n = p^k (eval_one_cyclotomic_not_prime_pow, eval_one_cyclotomic_prime_pow), and ev_{-1}(2 - q) = 3.
Record the discriminant remark (disc Phi_3 = -3, disc Phi_4 = -4, disc Phi_5 = 125) and the contrast over Q.
acceptance: 1/(2 - q) is not in sigma_1(Z[q]^N).
1/(1 + Phi_3) is not in sigma_{zeta_3}(Z[q]^N): ev_1(1 + Phi_3) = 4.
q - zeta_3 is not in sigma_{zeta_3}(Z[q]^N), even modulo (q - zeta_3)^2.

nodes.title: The cyclotomic completion of a module, and its exactness
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, a set S of positive integers and an R-module M, the cyclotomic completion of M is M[q]^S = lim_{f in Phi*_S} M[q]/f M[q], where M[q] is the R[q]-module of polynomials with coefficients in M and Phi*_S is the multiplicative monoid generated by the cyclotomic polynomials Phi_n, n in S (Habiro §7.3, where M is any abelian group; the completion depends only on the underlying abelian group, and an R-module structure makes it an R[q]^S-module). With the inverse-limit topology it is a complete separated topological R[q]^S-module with continuous scalar action, the kernel of each projection to M[q]/f M[q] is the submodule f M[q]^S, and for M = R it is the ring R[q]^S. The functor M -> M[q]^S from R-modules to R[q]^S-modules is EXACT for every R and every S, with no further hypothesis: M[q]/f M[q] is M tensored over R with R[q]/(f), which is a free R-module because f is monic, so every finite level is exact, and a cofinal chain in Phi*_S gives an R-linear isomorphism, natural in M, of M[q]^S with a countable product of copies of M, so no derived-limit term occurs. The functor commutes with arbitrary products, hence with finite direct sums; it does not commute with infinite direct sums, and the comparison map from M tensor_R R[q]^S is bijective for finitely presented M but not in general. Non-exactness appears only for the completion of R[q]-modules that are not of the form M[q] (modules with f-torsion); that is the derived completion owned by HabiroRings HR.2 and is not constructed here.
hypotheses: R is commutative and unital; S is any set of positive integers (for S empty, Phi*_S = {1} and the completion is zero).
M is any R-module; in Habiro's generality any abelian group, with the Z-module structure.
Phi*_S is countable and directed by divisibility, so it has a cofinal chain 1 = g_0 | g_1 | g_2 | ...; all limits may be computed along it.
Exactness is asserted for sequences of R-modules M, i.e. for the polynomial modules M[q]; completion of an arbitrary R[q]-module is not exact and is not treated here.
proofSteps: Define M[q]^S as the compatible families (x_f), x_f in M[q]/f M[q], f in Phi*_S, with the action of R[q]^S = lim R[q]/(f) levelwise; for M = R this is R[q]^S (Habiro §7.3, compatibility sentence).

Identify M[q]/f M[q] with M tensor_R R[q]/(f); by division with remainder by the monic f (mathlib Polynomial.modByMonic), R[q]/(f) is R-free with basis 1, q, ..., q^(deg f - 1) (the fact Habiro uses in the proof of Lemma 3.1). Hence each level is an exact functor of M commuting with arbitrary products.

For a cofinal chain 1 = g_0 | g_1 | ... the elements q^i g_j (j < k, 0 <= i < deg g_(j+1) - deg g_j) form compatible R-bases of the R[q]/(g_k); this gives an R-linear isomorphism M[q]^S = prod_j M^(deg g_(j+1) - deg g_j), natural in M. For S = N and g_k = P_k = (q;q)_k it is the normalised factorial expansion of HC.2 with coefficients in M.
Exactness: by the previous step M -> M[q]^S is a countable product of exact functors; equivalently, the kernel tower has surjective transition maps, so its lim^1 vanishes (Mittag-Leffler).

Multiplication by a monic f is injective on M[q], so f M[q] / g M[q] is M[q] / (g/f) M[q] for f | g; passing to the limit, the kernel of the projection to M[q]/f M[q] is f M[q]^S. Completeness, separatedness and continuity of the scalar action follow levelwise.
The comparison M tensor_R R[q]^S -> M[q]^S is the comparison M tensor_R prod R -> prod M under the isomorphism of step 3, bijective for finitely presented M.

Non-examples: for R = Z, S = N and M = Q the element sum_N P_N / N! (normalised coefficients 1/N!) is not in the image of Q tensor Z[q]^N; for M = the direct sum of countably many copies of Z with basis e_j, the element sum_j e_j P_j is not in the image of the direct sum of the Z[q]^N.
acceptance: For M = R the module completion is the ring R[q]^S.
For every short exact sequence of R-modules the completed sequence is exact; for 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/p -> 0 this gives Z[q]^N / p Z[q]^N = F_p[q]^N.

F_2[q]^N is not a domain: modulo (2, P_3), where P_3 = (1+q)^4 (1+q+q^2) mod 2, the idempotent separating the orders 2^k from the orders 3*2^k is q^5 + q + 1; so p Z[q]^N is not a prime ideal although Z[q]^N is a domain.
The kernel of the projection to M[q]/f M[q] is f M[q]^S.
M tensor_Z Z[q]^N -> M[q]^N is bijective for M = Z/p and not surjective for M = Q.
For the zero module, and for S empty, the completion is zero.

nodes.title: Injectivity of restriction for modules (Habiro Theorem 7.1)
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian group (or an R-module) and let S' be contained in S, both sets of positive integers. Write m <=>_A n when A = 0, or m = n, or m/n is a nonzero integer power of a prime p such that A is p-adically separated (the intersection of the p^j A is 0). If for every n in S there is a chain n' = n_0 <=>_A n_1 <=>_A ... <=>_A n_r = n (r >= 0) of elements of S starting at some n' in S', then the restriction rho^A_(S,S'): A[q]^S -> A[q]^(S') induced by the identity of A[q] is injective. The separation condition is that of A itself, not of any ring acting on A.
hypotheses: A is an abelian group; the completions are those of HC.5/the-completed-module.
The chain runs inside S and starts in S'; connectedness of S and S' separately is not enough.
The relation is taken over A: p-adic separatedness of A, not of the coefficient ring. The case m = n is included (see sourceIssues: the printed relation omits it; chains may omit such steps).
proofSteps: If A = 0 there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise let A' = Z ⊕ A with (m,a)(n,b) = (mn, mb + na). The ring A' is p-adically separated exactly when A is, so m <=>_A n iff m <=>_(A') n in the ring sense of HC.4/adjacency-of-orders.
Apply Theorem 4.1 (HC.4/injectivity-of-restriction) to A' to get injectivity of rho^(A')_(S,S').
By the direct-sum compatibility of HC.5/the-completed-module, A'[q]^S = Z[q]^S ⊕ A[q]^S compatibly with restriction, so rho^(A') = rho^Z ⊕ rho^A and rho^A is injective.
acceptance: For A = Z the statement is Theorem 4.1 over Z.

For the Z-module A = Z[1/p], S = {1, p}, S' = {1}: the hypothesis fails (A is not p-adically separated) and so does the conclusion: A[q]^{1,p} = Z[1/p][[q-1]] × Z[1/p][q]^{p} (Phi_1, Phi_p are comaximal once p is inverted) and rho^A kills the second factor.
For A = 0 every pair of orders is adjacent and all completions vanish.
For A = Q the relation is equality, so the hypothesis holds only when S' = S.

nodes.title: Chinese remainder decomposition under comaximality
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring and S = S_1 ⊔ S_2 a partition of a set of positive integers such that Phi_m and Phi_n generate the unit ideal of R[q] for every m in S_1 and n in S_2. Then the pair of restrictions R[q]^S -> R[q]^(S_1) × R[q]^(S_2) is an isomorphism of topological rings. For m ≠ n, Phi_m and Phi_n are comaximal in R[q] exactly when n/m is not an integer power of a prime, or n/m = p^e with e ≠ 0 and p a unit of R. More generally R[q]^S is the product of the R[q]^C over the classes C of the equivalence relation on S generated by non-comaximality, and if R ≠ 0 and there are at least two classes then R[q]^S has nontrivial idempotents and is not a domain. Comaximality is strictly stronger than non-adjacency: m and n fail to be adjacent as soon as R is not p-adically separated, which does not make p a unit; the two notions agree when R is a Noetherian domain (Krull intersection theorem), for example Z, Z[1/Δ], Q and F_p.
hypotheses: Cross pairs are comaximal in R[q]; non-adjacency alone is not sufficient (see the non-example).
R ≠ 0 for the idempotent and not-a-domain consequences.
Infinitely many classes are allowed; the product carries the product topology.
proofSteps: Comaximality criterion: for n/m not a prime power use Lemma 4.1(2); for n = m p^e use p in (Phi_m, Phi_n) (4.2) and Phi_n ≡ Phi_m^d mod p (4.1), so modulo p the ideal is generated by the monic Phi_m, which is the unit ideal only if R/p = 0.
Comaximality passes to powers and products, so f_1 and f_2 are comaximal for f_i in Phi*_(S_i), and R[q]/(f_1 f_2) = R[q]/(f_1) × R[q]/(f_2) (mathlib Ideal.quotientMulEquivQuotientProd).

Every f in Phi*_S factors as f_1 f_2 with f_i in Phi*_(S_i); pass to the limit over Phi*_S to get the isomorphism, and to the limit over finite subsets of S (Habiro (3.2)) for infinitely many classes.
Each class C gives a nonzero factor because R[q]^C maps onto R[q]/(Phi_n) ≠ 0 for n in C; the unit of that factor is a nontrivial idempotent.
For a Noetherian domain R and p not a unit, the intersection of the p^j R is 0 by Krull's theorem, so non-comaximality and adjacency coincide and the classes are the connected components of HC.4.

Non-example: R = Z × Q and S = {1, 2}. R is not 2-adically separated (the intersection of the 2^j R is 0 × Q), so 1 and 2 are not adjacent, but 2 is not a unit, Phi_1 and Phi_2 are not comaximal, and R[q]^{1,2} -> R[[q-1]] × R[[q+1]] is not surjective because its Z-component is not: ((3 - 2q)^-1, 0) is not in the image (Proposition 7.4(1), see HC.6/the-acceptance-examples).
acceptance: Z[q]^{1,6} = Z[[q-1]] × Z[q]^{6}, because Phi_6(1) = 1 so (q - 1, Phi_6) = (1) in Z[q]; hence Z[q]^{1,6} is not a domain.
Q[q]^{1,2} = Q[[q-1]] × Q[[q+1]], with idempotent e_1 ≡ (3 + 2q - q^2)/4 modulo (q-1)^2 (q+1); the same holds over Z[1/2] because Res(Phi_1, Phi_2) = 2.
Z[q]^{1,2} has no such decomposition: 1 and 2 are adjacent over Z and Z[q]^{1,2} is a domain.
Over R = Z × Q the set {1, 2} is not connected for adjacency, yet no product decomposition along it exists.

nodes.title: The ring Q[q]^S, and rings in which the orders are units
nodes.statement: Let R be a nonzero ring in which every element of S is a unit (for example R = Q). Then R[q]^S is isomorphic to the product over n in S of the Phi_n-adic completions R[q]^{n}. Consequently: R[q]^S is not a domain when S has at least two elements; for S' strictly contained in S the restriction R[q]^S -> R[q]^(S') is surjective and not injective; for S nonempty the evaluation map R[q]^S -> P_S(R) = prod_{n in S} R[q]/(Phi_n) is surjective and not injective. For R = Q and a root of unity ζ of order n in S, the expansion map Q[q]^S -> Q(ζ)[[q - ζ]] is the projection to Q[q]^{n} followed by an isomorphism Q[q]^{n} = Q(ζ)[[q - ζ]], so it is surjective, and not injective when S has another element. The map Z[q]^S -> Q[q]^S is injective (Lemma 3.1).
hypotheses: R ≠ 0 and every n in S is a unit of R (this is the source's parenthetical generalisation of §7.5).
S nonempty for the evaluation statement (for S empty both sides are the zero ring).

The identification Q[q]^{n} = Q(ζ)[[q - ζ]] is the standard fact that a local map of complete discrete valuation rings sending a uniformiser to a uniformiser and inducing an isomorphism of residue fields is an isomorphism; Phi_n is irreducible and separable over Q.

nodes.title: Inverting primes: the completions of Z[1/Δ][q], compared with Z and Q
nodes.statement: Let Δ ≥ 1 and R = Z[1/Δ] (R = Z[1/p] when Δ = p). Over R two distinct orders m, n are adjacent exactly when n/m is a nonzero power of a prime not dividing Δ; since R is a Noetherian domain this is also non-comaximality, and the classes of the positive integers are the sets S_a = {n : v_p(n) = a_p for every prime p dividing Δ}, one for each family a = (a_p). Hence: (1) R[q]^N is the product of the R[q]^(S_a), infinitely many nonzero factors when Δ > 1, so it is not a domain although R is; each S_a is connected, so restriction from R[q]^(S_a) to any nonempty subset is injective, and restriction from R[q]^N to a set S' of orders is injective exactly when S' meets every S_a; in particular the expansion map at q = 1 and the restriction to {1} are injective over Z and not over R. (2) Evaluation at all roots of unity, R[q]^N -> P_N(R), is still injective (Theorem 6.1 on each factor, with n = prod_p p^(a_p) and the infinitely many adjacent orders n ℓ, ℓ a prime not dividing Δ), whereas over Q it is not; evaluation on a set of orders missing some S_a is not injective. (3) For a root of unity ζ of order n prime to Δ the expansion map is injective on the factor R[q]^(S_0) of orders prime to Δ (Theorem 5.2: the odd primes dividing n, and 2 when 4 | n, are not inverted) and zero on every other factor. (4) Z[q]^N -> R[q]^N is injective, but Z[q]^N[1/Δ] -> R[q]^N is not surjective: its image is a domain and contains no nontrivial idempotent. So neither the domain property nor connectedness passes from the coefficient ring to the completion, and completion does not commute with inverting Δ.

nodes.title: Each factor of Z[1/Δ][q]^N is a domain
nodes.statement: Let R = Z[1/Δ] and let S_a be a class of HC.5/inverting-a-prime-and-the-rational-case. Then R[q]^(S_a) is an integral domain, and for every n in S_a and every primitive n-th root of unity ζ the expansion map R[q]^(S_a) -> R[ζ][[q - ζ]] is injective. So R[q]^N is a product of integral domains, as GSWZ Remark 1.2 states for the number-field Habiro ring. For factors whose orders are divisible by an odd prime dividing Δ this is not covered by Theorem 5.2, whose separation hypothesis fails there.
hypotheses: R = Z[1/Δ], n in S_a; ζ lies in the algebraic closure of Q.
The argument is Galois descent and is this packet's own; Habiro proves only the case covered by Theorem 5.2.
proofSteps: Restriction from R[q]^(S_a) to R[q]^{n} is injective by Theorem 4.1, because S_a is connected over R; so it suffices to treat R[q]^{n}.
Let R'' = R[ζ_n]. By Lemma 3.1, R[q]^{n} -> R''[q]^{n} is injective, and R''[q]^{n} is the completion at the linear factors q - ζ', ζ' primitive of order n (Habiro, p. 1136).

Two primitive n-th roots either differ by a unit of R'' (their ratio has order not a prime power, or a power of a prime dividing Δ) or are adjacent over R'' (ratio of order ℓ^k with ℓ not dividing Δ, and R'' is ℓ-adically separated). So R''[q]^{n} is the product of the completions at the connected classes of roots (Chinese remainder), and each factor embeds into a power series ring R''[[q - ζ']] by Theorem 5.1, hence is a domain (HC.4/connectedness-of-primitive-roots).

The Galois group of Q(ζ_n)/Q acts on R''[q]^{n}, fixes the image of R[q]^{n} and permutes the classes transitively. If f g = 0 in R[q]^{n}, then on one class the component of f or of g vanishes; by Galois invariance it vanishes on all classes, so f = 0 or g = 0.
The same argument shows that the expansion at any ζ of order n is injective on R[q]^{n}, hence on R[q]^(S_a).

(4) The Kontsevich series F = sum_{n ≥ 0} (q;q)_n is the compatible family of the sums of (q;q)_n over n < N modulo P_N; its normalised coefficients are all 1; its values are F(1) = 1, F(-1) = 3, F(ω) = 5 - ω, F(i) = 8 - 3i, F(ζ_5) = 9 - 5ζ_5 - 3ζ_5^2, F(ζ_6) = 17 - 13ζ_6, each computed from the truncation at N = ord ζ and unchanged for larger N; its expansion at q = 1 is sum_k (-1)^k ξ_k (q - 1)^k with ξ = 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 53, 217, 1014, 5335, 31240, ... (the Fishburn numbers), the coefficient of (q-1)^k depending only on the terms n ≤ k; its expansion at q = -1 begins 3 + 11(q+1) + 72(q+1)^2 + 635(q+1)^3 + 7085(q+1)^4, the coefficient of (q+1)^k depending only on n ≤ 2k + 1; at ω it begins (5 - ω) + (49 + 40ω)(q - ω) + (128 + 693ω)(q - ω)^2. F and the constant 1 have the same value at q = 1 and different expansions there. (5) q^-1 = sum_{n ≥ 0} q^n (q;q)_n (Proposition 7.1), with normalised coefficients q^n and the exact identity q times the sum over n < N equals 1 - (q;q)_N; its value at ζ is ζ^-1 and its expansion at 1 is sum_k (-1)^k (q-1)^k. (7) The geometric series sum q^n is not an element: its partial sums take the value N at q = 1, so they are not Cauchy, and 1 - q is not a unit.
